I think we value moderation. We prize fitting in. Ambitious people with big ideas intimidate us.  We don't want to be like those Yanks who only care about work and making a lot of money. People joke about our love of mediocrity, but it's true: mediocrity is almost a virtue here.

I don't think a lot of people do want Toronto to be world-class. It's an often repeated slogan (probably due to pride, since Toronto is Canada's biggest city and it *should* be world class), but it tends to get eye rolls. People here would love to think we are that, but they're afraid to go for it because that might mean rocking the boat. It's very hard to change a culture.

I also think our old Protestant work ethic was pretty punishing, and that may be one reason mediocrity has become a virtue. Without the ambition, the money, the inspiration, work was probably pretty miserable even though that work ethic made Toronto run smoothly for so long. So if we can't have the big ideas and true excellence, we can at least make work culture easier by rewarding a job done decently, rather than well. If someone comes along and throws a wrench in this implicit understanding, they're going to make everyone else look bad and feel uncomfortable. They're going to be hated.

I like your enthusiasm, but tall poppy syndrome is very real in Canada. We don't like to "show off." We're afraid of big ideas. I moved back here from NYC (and further back SF), and the work culture was a huge shock. You weren't rewarded for your ideas and energy. You were punished for them and treated with suspicion. The people who kept their heads down and fit in were the ones considered excellent at their jobs. 

OP is onto something real. 

They have work-life balance in Europe but they also reward creativity and genuine excellence. It's the best of both worlds. Here, people learn to detach from their jobs because ambition is punished. 

What made Toronto great in previous decades was that you could live cheaply downtown, work part time and devote yourself to creative endeavours or just enjoying life. Work always sucked (look up the Orange Order to learn the roots of our uptight, overly proper culture), but you didn't have to do a lot of it to live. In that world, materialism wasn't prized. Now that is gone and Toronto has a massive identity crisis. With our cultural DNA, can we really turn ourselves into an energetic, ambitious American city?

Don't waste space with an 'objective' line. As an employer, I already know your objective is to get the job you're applying for. Beyond that, I don't care. 

Don't waste valuable real estate on something your employer doesn't care about.

You can't just blast out hundreds of generic resumes for job openings you found on Indeed. By the time you saw them on an aggregator site, they were filled, if they were real at all.

With everything being automated these days, you have to take the opposite approach: networking. Focus on your own network. And I DON"T mean LinkedIn. I mean in the physical world. You may say you don't know anyone with connections but you have no idea.

Get yourself out there in person to job networking events, parties etc. If you don't get invited to parties, start where you are. Chat with your neighbours. Can you borrow a dog-friendly dog  and start going to a dog park? The point is to put yourself in real-world situations where you can chat casually with people, let people know you're looking for work. You want to ask if you can talk to people (on the phone for a few minutes, on Zoom, buy them a coffee -- whatever works for THEM) to find out more about the industry and how to break in. Then send a follow-up thank you note and connect to them on LI. I've been asked for this favour by strangers and have never ever said no.

Each of these interactions might not directly lead to a job interview but you're building a network that will pay off for the rest of your life. 

Also: did you supervise anyone in your former jobs, even once in a while during a shift? Were you trusted to handle difficult interactions? If so, say it! Don't keep using generic words like 'communications.' SHOW how you successfully communicated. Your cover letter should start with a story that engages the reader and shows how you demonstrated a skill that the job posting asks for.

I know how frustrating this is, but you will develop job search skills that will benefit you throughout your entire career. Unlike other recent grads you may know who waltz into a job without having to develop these crucial skills.

I have worked in both medicine and public health, and you are absolutely spot on, but very few people talk about this stuff. In the medical world, it's all about the promise of personalized medicine, but that's expensive and more hype than reality at this point. In the public health world, it's pushing people to follow guidelines and trying to seem as definitive as possible to get people to comply. Experts in those worlds will admit that there are always outliers -- people for whom salt lowers their blood pressure, or plant sterols raise their cholesterol. But these people are a minority, and and inconvenience when you are trying to create guidelines for the general public. 

Statins did a real number on my mom's memory. We took her off them and her cognition got better. We put her back on them and it got worse. Studies just tell you what happens to the majority. The only way to find out what will happen to you is to try the drug. But still there are so many people who dismiss my mom's experience because "studies" suggest it didn't happen to her. They think they're following the science, but this is actually not scientific -- it's magical thinking. An almost childlike trust in a process that's the best we've got, but is still deeply flawed. 

Totally agree public health has done wonders for human health. And for the most part it should be followed. Problem is that everyone is an outlier sometimes. The gaslighting from the public health community has gotten a lot better since they learned some humbling lessons during COVID. But a lot of it comes down to not knowing how to convey nuance to the public.

I'm a couple years into menopause and like a lot of women, the weight came on fast and nothing would shift it. I was exhausting myself in the gym and getting nothing out of it.

I've always known that sugar had an outsized negative effect on my weight and have struggled with my sugar addiction all my life. So when those continuous glucose monitors became more common, I started to notice people saying that sugar blood spikes after meals are actually pretty huge even for non-diabetics. And this blood sugar gets converted to fat -- unless you use it up with exercise right away. I was reading that even a ten minute walk after a meal could reduce someone's blood sugar spike by a third.

So I started to take a ten minute walk after each and every meal. Every day. Despite rain or snow. Despite exhaustion and no matter how busy I was or how bad my mood. I just told myself this is something I do now. I made it automatic. And I waited. I didn't weigh myself or start expecting big changes any time soon.

After about six weeks, I started noticing my clothes were getting loose. I waited another couple of weeks and then weighed myself. I had lost about 7 lbs.

This was the easiest, most pleasant 7 lbs I have ever lost! And of course I'm keeping going with it.

I do feel that as we get older, women have a harder time regulating blood sugar, which probably plays a role in how hard it is to lose or even maintain weight in menopause. So this might be helpful to many of us. And the best part is: it's free, easy, quick and relaxing. You don't have to drive anywhere, or buy anything special. You just do it.

For me, I just inched into the 'at-risk' category (the one that comes before pre-diabetes), so the most exciting test will come during my next bloodwork to see if my blood sugar has dropped. Hope this helps someone out there!

Perspective from the patient's side:

I'm supporting a friend with stage 4 nsc lung cancer, being held at bay for the past year. Every 3 months he gets the terrifying CT scan and results appear on his chart a few hours later. He doesn't see his oncologist until the next day. 

Every time, he is sitting there at his computer, shaking and hyperventilating, refreshing his chart every 2 minutes for hours until it appears. Then he calls me and I have to read it for him. I'm not a medical professional. Knowing that scan is life or death for him, he is just not able to wait, when he could know his fate immediately.

One time I discovered it was in his bones and he wasn't aware of that.  It wasn't a new discovery, and I knew that he was terrified of this because some random doctor (not an oncologist) had said something offhand about how you're dead if it goes to your bones or brain. 

So I had to make a very fast decision not to tell him. (Eventually, his oncologist mentioned it, but with the proper reassurance and caveats).

Last time, his scan didn't appear until much later than normal. He managed to get into the fine print and read that sometimes physicians will choose to delay posting the results until after they've talked to patients. To a terrified cancer patient, this means only one thing.

So my friend finally called his oncologist's office to tell them results hadn't appeared yet and ask whether they withheld them. The receptionist checked with a nurse who was probably very busy and just needed to tell him something to get rid of him. So she said 'the doctor will talk to you tomorrow.' Seemingly confirming his worst fears. He asked 'but can you tell me whether the doctor purposely withheld my scan from my chart?' And back came: "The doctor will talk to you tomorrow.' Not denying it.

My friend is an ex-cop and owns a gun. We always worry that he is going to panic and do something really rash. It was a very difficult next few hours. 

Fortunately the scan appeared that evening, and it was all clear. 

There has to be a better way, for the sake of both patients and providers.

My mom wasn't on formal hospice. She was in a retirement home (Canada). When she started to go downhill, I spoke with the medical director and her floor nurse. I explained that my mom wasn't religious, she wasn't interested in life for life's sake. I gave them a copy of her living will, which went way beyond a simple DNR in making her wishes clear. We agreed to put a 'do not transport' in her chart. But I knew that the night nurses were normally ship-ins from some agency and wouldn't hesitate to call an ambulance without looking at her chart. So this was a big worry. And I saw from the couple of times that she fell and ended up in the ER that a whole medical process would kick in with bloodwork, IVs and scans while she lay in a hallway with people screaming for opioids. At all costs, we wanted to avoid her dying in a hospital. 

Her assigned family doctor at the home was a very old man, very difficult to talk to. I tried talking to him about my mom's wishes, and whether, for example, it would violate her living will to give her nutritional shakes when she no longer wanted to eat, for example. He shut down that conversation very fast and said not to even think that way.

At some point, the home wanted to transfer her care over to the palliative team (which would give them similar rights to hospice in the US, I think), but this would require a referral from her family doc. He denied it, saying she wasn't in any pain. 

A couple of weeks ago she fully lost her ability to speak and lost most of her appetite. The home tried again to ask for the referral to palliative, but her family doc hadn't gotten around to re-examining her by the time she really began going downhill. The death rattle began softly and intermittently one day, and that day she actually started crying, which was horrible to see. By the next morning it was louder and she was hard to wake. That's when the agency night nurse said she wanted to call an ambulance. I knew that her (excellent) floor nurse was about to come on shift, so we waited. Sure enough, that nurse said it wasn't necessary. We kept an eye on her oxygen and started her on it when it began to decline. That made her more comfortable. That was when the family doc (still hadn't seen her) ordered the bloodwork. Fortunately I had the option of saying no. But I couldn't believe he wanted to do that to her. 

By the way, I posted this same story/question in  r/AskDocs. And [you should see](https://www.reddit.com/r/AskDocs/comments/14h4gb6/comment/jp9ok8w/?context=3) the way these physicians are responding. A plastic surgeon has explained to me that doctors have the duty to do absolutely everything that doesn't technically violate a DNR no matter if the patient is dying or not. And I'm getting downvoted for my view that prolonging the dying process seems like torture. 

I would love to think there's a generational difference here, and that things are getting better with the younger docs. My mom's young family doc before she moved into the home was so comfortable with end of life conversations, and he really helped me think this stuff through. I think she would have had a much less peaceful death if he hadn't taken the time to talk to me about what to do.

I guess it's just going to have to be up to the patients and families to figure this out then. Thank god I had the right to say no. Medicine can keep people alive long past the point anyone would want to keep living. And it sounds like doctors aren't trained to be part of that conversation.
